label: Heuristic style list, not an AI detector. It names stock phrases and patterns that readers often associate with machine-drafted social posts. A match does not show that a text was written by a model, and a clean result does not show that it was written by a person. No accuracy is claimed.
matching: Phrases match case-insensitively on whole words: 'delve' matches 'Delve' but not 'Delvecchio'. Inflected forms that are also tells are listed explicitly. Straight and curly apostrophes are equal, a space matches any run of whitespace and a hyphen also matches a space.

tells.reason: Rare in everyday social writing and widely mocked as a sign of machine-drafted text; say 'look at' or just start.
Generic scene-setting that tells the reader nothing; open with the specific thing that happened.
Stock hype word; show the concrete before-and-after instead.
Template marketing verb phrase; name what the reader can actually do now.
Filler transition before the content starts; cut it and give the first point.
Common in technical writing, but overused in generated posts; fine if it is how you talk.
Formulaic announcement opener; lead with what changed and why it matters to the reader.
Ornamental phrasing rarely used in posts written quickly by a person.
Padding that announces importance instead of showing it; state the point directly.
Abstract journey metaphor; name the actual problem.
Vague promise of improvement; say by how much or in what way.
Buzzwords that generated text uses heavily; keep only the ones you would say out loud.
Essay-style wrap-up that rarely belongs in a short post.
Assistant-style sign-off; end with the useful link or the specific question.

phrases: let me know in the comments
tells.reason: Generic engagement prompt; a specific question gets better replies and avoids engagement-bait patterns.
Suspense filler before a point that could just be stated.
The 'it's not just X, it's Y' contrast is one of the most recognised generated-text templates.
'No X, no Y, just Z' is a stock rhythm; one plain sentence usually reads better.
Several em dashes in one post are an often-cited tell; commas, full stops or brackets read more like most people's writing.
Repeated three-item lists ('fast, simple, and secure') give text a templated rhythm.
Repeated rocket and sparkle emoji are a common decoration in generated launch posts.
Every line starting with an emoji is a recognisable template layout.
Opening with a rhetorical question is a common template; a concrete first line usually says more.
A long block of hashtags reads as generated and some networks limit them; keep the few that describe the post.
Many exclamation marks read as forced enthusiasm.
